text: pr. Statius to his Pollius, greeting.

To you at least, sweetest Pollius—and most worthy of that repose to which you cling so faithfully—I have no need to commend at length the boldness of these little books, since you know that many of them were born suddenly in your own bosom, and have often dreaded this audacity of my pen, as often as, drawn aside into the sanctuary of your own eloquence, I go more deeply into letters and am led by you into every recess of study. Secure, therefore, this third book of our Silvae is sent to you. The second indeed had you as its witness, but this one has you as its author. For Hercules of Surrentum opens its first threshold—the Hercules consecrated on your shore, whom, as soon as I had seen him, I worshipped in these verses. There follows the little book in which I thus escorted the most splendid and to me most delightful young man, Maecius Celer, sent by our most sacred Emperor to the Syrian legion, since I could not follow him. The devotion of my Claudius Etruscus, too, deserved some consolation from our studies, while he mourned his aged father with true tears—which is now a most rare thing. Earinus, moreover, the freedman of our Germanicus—you know how long I delayed my response to his desire—when he had asked that I dedicate in verse his hair, which he was sending in a doubled casket, with a mirror, to the Pergamene Asclepius. The last is the eclogue in which I urge my own Claudia to retire with me to Naples. Here, if I speak truly, is conversation, and indeed unguarded, as with a wife, and one who would rather persuade than please. To this little book in particular you will show favour, since you know that this resolve for my repose is aimed especially at you, and that I am retiring not so much to my homeland as to you. Farewell.

1. Hercules of Surrentum, belonging to Pollius Felix
Pollius renews for you, Tirynthian, the interrupted rites,
and assigns the reasons for the year's delay:
that you are worshipped now in a greater dome, and no longer hold,
poor, a bare shore and a roof habitable by wandering sailors,
but gleaming doorposts and gables propped up with Greek
metals, as though, purified again by the torches of an honest
fire, you were climbing the heavens from the Oetaean flame.
Scarce is there faith for eyes and mind: are you that inglorious
keeper of an open threshold and a small altar?
Whence this new hall and unlooked-for splendour for rustic
Alcides? There are fates of gods, there are fates of places!
O swift devotion! Here, lately, one might see barren sands,
a mountain's flank sprinkled by the sea, and rocks shaggy with thorns,
and ground that would suffer no footsteps. What fortune suddenly
enriched the stiff crags? Did these walls come at a Tyrian quill
or a Getic lyre? The year itself is amazed at the labours,
and the cramped months, in their twelvefold bound,
marvel at the long-lived work. A god brought the citadels
and reared up his own, and the resisting rocks
he removed, straining, and with his great breast pushed back
the mountain: you would believe he had bidden his cruel stepmother.
So come, whether, now free of the laws, you dwell in your father's
Argos and tread upon Eurystheus sunk in his tomb,
or whether you hold the throne of your own Jove and the stars
won by your valour, and Hebe, girded, holds out to you
a draught of blessed nectar, better than the rejected Phrygian:
come hither and bring your genius to the rising temple.
Not harmful Lerna, nor the fields of poor Molorchus,
nor the dreaded field of Nemea and the Thracian caves
demand you, nor the polluted altars of the Egyptian king,
but a happy and simple house, ignorant of evil
frauds, and a seat most worthy of heavenly guests.
Lay aside your savage bows and the cruel troop of your quiver
and the club drenched with the blood of many kings,
and let go from your great shoulders the foe spread upon them:
here for you a lofty couch is woven with Sidonian
acanthus, and the bed grows rough with ivory figures.
Come appeased and gentle, not turbulent with anger
nor fearing servitude, but such as Maenalian Auge
detained you, spent with revels and dripping with much wine,
and such as Thespius, your father-in-law so many times over,
beheld in amazement after the crimes of a wandering night. Here for you a festive
wrestling-school, and the innocent rages of youths without the gauntlet,
hold their yearly contests in a swift cycle.
Here a priest is inscribed in the temple, his grandfather rejoicing,
small as yet and like to you, when with your first hand
you crushed the stepmother's monsters and grieved them slain.
But what were the beginnings of the sudden temple, venerable one,
tell me, come, Calliope; Alcides as your ally will sound
the great strain, and his measures will be changed for the strung bow.
It was the time when the most scorching axis of heaven
leans upon the lands, and Sirius, struck by much Hyperion,
keen, sets the panting fields ablaze,
and now the day was at hand on which, fit for fugitive kings,
the Arician grove of Trivia smokes, and with much torchlight
the lake that knows of Hippolytus shines; Diana herself crowns
her deserving dogs and wipes her darts
and lets the beasts go safe, and the whole Italian land,
its hearths chaste, keeps the Ides of Hecate holy.
But I, although beneath the hills of Dardanian Alba
I had my own estate, and the water running by the gift
of the great leader sufficed at home to soothe my cares and ease
the heats, was guesting at the rocks known by the Sirens' name
and the home of eloquent Pollius, no stranger,
ever learning the man's ways and his peace and the new
flowers of the Muses and his untouched songs.
By chance, while we kept Trivia's day on the wet shore
and, heavy, shunned the narrow doors and accustomed roofs
and warded off the sun with leaves and a spreading tree,
the sky hid itself, and the bright light gave way to sudden
clouds, and the west wind, thinned, with a heavier south wind
grew wet; such a cloud as Saturn's daughter brought
to Libya, while rich Elissa was given to her Ilian
husband, and the nymphs, as witnesses, howled through the wilds.
We scattered, and the slaves snatch away the festive feasts
and the garlanded wines: nor was there anywhere for the banquet to move,
although countless houses settled above the rejoicing
fields and the mountain shone rich with many a roof:
but the threatening clouds urged us to seek the nearest place,
and the faith of fair weather, hurt, that would return.
There stood a slender hut, called by the name of a sacred temple,
and a small home pressed great Alcides in a humble dwelling,
scarce able to cover the wave-wandering sailors
and the searchers of the deep. Hither all our crowd we gathered,
hither the feast and the rich couches and the throng of servants
are packed, and the most welcome band of bright Polla.
The doors did not hold us, and the narrow shrine fell short.
The god blushed and laughed, and entered the beloved heart
of Pollius, and embraced the man with coaxing arms.
'Are you,' he said, 'that bestower of wealth, who with lavish mind
filled at once the houses of Dicarchus and youthful
Parthenope? Who fixed for my mountain so many gables,
so many green groves, so many rocks imitating faces,
and bronzes, so many waxes living with painted light?
For what was this house, what this land, before
it could rejoice in you? Along a long track you covered
the bare crags, and where there was only a footpath,
now a high portico stands for you with set-out columns,
that the way might not be mean. The shores of the curving coast
you shut, with twin domes enclosing the warm nymphs.
Scarce could I count your works; to me alone is Pollius poor and needy:
yet glad I enter such a home,
and the shore that you spread out I love. But the next seat
looks down on this, and Juno secretly laughs at my threshold.
Give me a temple and altars worthy of your endeavours,
which ships would not wish to pass even with favouring sails,
whither the ethereal father and the summoned throng of gods
at the feast may come, and from a lofty temple his hostess-sister.
Nor let it terrify you that the solid boss of the grudging
mountain stands stiff against you and is never worn away by measureless age:
I myself will be present and aid such great endeavours
and break through the rough entrails of the unwilling earth.
Begin, and, trusting in Hercules' urgings, dare.
Not more swiftly stood the Amphionian citadels
or the Pergamean labour.' He spoke and left his mind behind.
And no delay: when the weapon is shaped by the written design,
countless hands came together: theirs the care to cut the woods
and lift the beams, theirs to sink
the foundations in the soil. Part of the damp earth is baked,
to protect against winters and shut out frosts,
and the untamed flint melts in the curving furnace.
But the chief labour is to hew away with the hand
the opposing cliffs and the rocks that refuse the iron.
Here the father of the place himself, the Tirynthian, his arms laid aside,
sweats, and with strong axe the deformed ground,
when the heavy sky is overspread with the shade of night,
he himself digs, and the rich Goat-rocks and green Taurubulae
echo back, and a huge echo of the sea returns to the lands.
Not so loud does Aetna sound with its moving anvils,
when Brontes and Steropes strike, nor is the crash greater
from the Lemnian caves, when fiery Mulciber lets fall
the aegis and adorns Pallas with chaste gifts.
The crags shrink, and, returned under the rosy light,
the craftsmen marvel at the work. Scarce does a second year
pant out, and the rich Tirynthian from his huge citadel
looks down on the waves and challenges the roof of his joined
stepmother, and invites Pallas to worthy temples.
Now the peaceful trumpets give their signals, now the sand,
burning, smokes for the brave rites: these honours neither the Pisaean
Jove nor the father of shady Cirrha would disdain.
Nothing is sad in these places; let lamentable Isthmos give way,
let grim Nemea give way: here a happier child offers sacrifice.
The green Nereids themselves spring out of their own accord
from their pumice caves: they cling to the wet crags
and are not ashamed to watch in secret the naked wrestling-schools.
And Gaurus watches, wooded with Icarian vine,
and the grove that crowns Nesis fixed in the sea,
and calm Limon and Euploea, an omen for ships,
and Lucrine Venus, and from the Phrygian summit you, Misenum,
shall learn the Greek trumpets, and kindly Parthenope
laughs at the native rite and the naked
contests of men and the small images of her own crown.
Come too and yourself, glad, deign with unconquered hand
the deeds of your own contest; whether to cleave the clouds with the discus,
or to outstrip the swift west winds with the javelin,
or whether it is sweet to you to knot the Libyan wrestling-bouts by hand,
indulge the rites, and, if you have apples to spare
from the Hesperides, set them in the venerable lap of Polla;
for she can hold, and will not so far degrade the honour.
But if she could take back her sweet glory and her green years,
—give me pardon, Alcides—you might perhaps have spun for her your thread.
These things I, glad and revelling at the rising altars,
brought as my offerings. Now on the very threshold—I see
him loosing his voice and uttering such words:
'A blessing on your spirit and your wealth, you who imitate my labours,
who tame the stiff cliffs and the shameful wastes
of barren nature, and turn to use
the lairs haunted by wild beasts, and bring forth foully hidden
powers; what rewards for your deserts shall I now pay you?
What thanks shall I render? I will hold the threads of the Fates
and draw out the distaffs—I know how to conquer hard Death—,
I will turn away your mourning and forbid sad losses,
and you, unharmed, I will renew with green old age,
and grant you long to behold your young grandsons,
until both this one is ripe for a bride and that one for a husband,
and again from them a new brood and a forward band
now creep over their grandsire's shoulders, now in a coaxing throng
race vying to the kisses of calm Polla.
For to my temples a bound of years shall never be set,
while the engine of the flaming sky carries me,
nor shall there be more dear to me Nemea and ancient Argos
nor the Tiburtine house and the chambers of the sun, Gades.'
So he speaks; and touching the fire rising on the altars
and shaking his temples white with poplar foliage,
he swore by the Styx and the thunderbolts of the ethereal father.

2. Propempticon for Maecius Celer
Gods, whose love it is to keep the bold keels safe
and to soothe the savage perils of the windy deep,
spread the sea soft and turn to my vows a calm
will, and let no gentle wave drown out the one who prays:
'A great and rare deposit, Neptune, we give to your deep,
a young man is entrusted to the doubtful main,
Maecius, and he prepares to carry across the seas the greater
part of our soul. Bring forth your kindly
stars and settle on the twin horns of the yard-arm,
sons of Oebalus; for you let sea and sky
shine: far off drive the stormy stars
of your Ilian sister, I pray, and shut them from all the sky.
You too, dark-blue band of the sea, Nereids,
to whom honour and the fortune of the second realm has fallen
—if it be lawful for me to name the great sea's stars—,
rise from the glassy caves of foaming Doris,
and the bays of Baiae and the shores teeming with warm waves
vie in a calm swimming to circle round.
Seeking where the high ship is, which the noble nursling
of warlike Ausonia, Celer, rejoices to climb.
Nor is it long to seek: but lately, beyond the seas,
the first to land at the Dicarchean shores the heavy Egyptian year,
the first to salute Capreae, and on the right margin
sprinkled the Mareotic wines of Tyrrhenian Minerva.
Gird each side of this ship in your soft circle,
and, your tasks shared out, you stretch the hempen
cables of the mast, you bind the topsails to the highest yards,
you open the sails to the west winds; let part replace the benches,
part lower into the waters the rudders of the curving stern;
let there be those for whom the heavy lead-plummet explores the depths,
and those who tie astern the boat that will follow
and pluck up from deep within the hooked anchor-cables;
let one temper the tides and bend the sea toward the dawn:
let none of the grey-green sisters be free of her office;
hence let Proteus, with much body, and Triton, with twin body,
swim ahead, and Glaucus, who lost his loins to sudden
monsters, as often as he glides to his fatherland's shores,
striking shore-loving Anthedon with his coaxing tail.
But you above all, Palaemon, with your divine mother,
assent, if it is my love to lay open your Thebes,
and I sing of Phoebean Amphion with no degenerate quill.
And the father who breaks the winds in his Aeolian prison,
to whom the varied blasts and every breath through the seas
of the world and the storms and the rain-clouds obey,
let him press Boreas and Eurus and Notus more closely,
the mountain set against them: let the sky be free for Zephyr alone,
let him alone drive the ships and skim above the highest waves,
unceasing on the sea; until, with no whirlwind,
he assigns your glad sails to the Paraetonian banks.'
We are heard. He himself calls the ship and chides the lingering
sailors. Lo, my heart already with timid cold
slips down, and I cannot, though the horror of the omen warns me,
close the tears suspended on the margin of my eyes.
And now the sailor has parted the ship from land with the cable loosed
and let down the narrow gangway into the sea.
The savage master from the stern with a long shout
scatters the embraces and tears apart the faithful kisses,
nor is it allowed to linger long on the dear neck,
yet I will go onto the land last of all the throng,
nor depart until the ship is already withdrawing.
Who made for wretched living creatures this rough and severed
sea a path, and drove the pious nurslings of the solid earth
out into the waves and sent them into the gaping deep,
bold in his ingenuity? For no rasher was that valour
which joined cold Pelion to the summit of Ossa
and twice pressed panting Olympus beneath the ridges.
Was it so little to cross the slow marshes
and pools, and to set narrow rivers beneath bridges?
We go into the sheer abyss, and from every side flee
our native lands, shut in a scanty plank and a bare sky.
Hence the fury of the winds and the indignant storms
and the roaring of the sky and the more thunderbolts for the Thunderer.
Before ships the seas were torpid in sluggish sleep,
nor did Thetis dare to foam, nor the waves to scatter clouds:
the waters swelled at the sight of the keels,
and the storm rose against man. Then the Pleiades were cloudy,
and the Olenian Goat; then Orion was worse than his wont.
I complain justly: see, the ship, driven through the wandering waves,
flees, little by little smaller, and far off conquers
my keeping eyes, holding so many fears clasped in its slender wood.
And you who above the rest, pledge of our love,
will carry, Celer—with what heart shall I now bear my sleep
or how endure my days? What messenger to one fearing
everything, whether the smooth wave has let you pass
the raging mouth of the Lucanian sea, whether twisted Charybdis
heaves, or the ravaging maiden of the Sicilian deep,
what manners headlong Hadria bears to you in your course,
what peace there is in the Carpathian, with what breeze
Doris carries you up, flattered by the thefts of the Agenorean bull?
But I have deserved my complaints. For why, when you sought the camp,
did I not go, an eager comrade, even to the unknown
Indians and Cimmerian chaos? My king's warlike standards
would stand near, whether you held weapons in your hand or the reins,
or gave laws to the armed; and of your works,
though not a partner, surely an admirer I would be present.
If once Phoenix, reverend to great Achilles,
came to the Ilian shore and Thymbraean Pergamus,
unwarlike and sworn to nothing for the swelling son of Atreus,
why is my love a coward? But with faithful heart
I shall never be absent, and shall follow your sails with long vows.
Isis, once stabled beneath the caves of Phoroneus,
now queen of Pharos and divinity of the panting East,
receive with many-sounding sistrum the Mareotic ship,
and the excellent young man, to whom the Latin leader gave
the Eastern standards and the Palestinian cohorts to rein,
yourself with calm hand lead through the festive thresholds and the sacred
harbours and your cities. With you as guide let him learn
whence comes the fertile licence of the marshy Nile,
why the shoals subside and the bank confines the waters
that are pooled with Cecropian mud, why grudging Memphis,
or why the mouth of Therapnaean Canopus is wanton,
why the Lethean doorkeeper guards the Egyptian altars,
why cheap animals are equal to the great gods;
what altars the long-lived Phoenix spreads for itself,
what fields it deigns, or in what flood of Nile
the adored Apis plunges, to the alarm of trembling shepherds.
Lead him too to the Emathian shades, where the warlike founder
of the city, drenched with Hyblaean nectar, endures,
and the serpent-bearing house, where, sunk in coaxing poison,
the Actian Cleopatra fled the Ausonian chains.
On even to the Assyrian seats and the appointed camps
escort him, and to Latin Mars, goddess, hand over the young man,
nor will he be a new guest: as a boy he sweated in these fields,
known as yet only by the light of the broader stripe,
yet brave already to outstrip the squadrons with an easy wheel
and to condemn the Eastern arrows with his javelin.
Therefore there shall be that day, on which, about to give you greater things,
Caesar shall bid you depart from your finished war,
and we, again standing on this shore, shall behold the vast
waves and shall beg for other breezes.
O how great I shall be then, or how great the votive lyre
I shall move with my quill! When, my neck bound with a great band,
you lift me on your shoulders, and first upon my breast,
new from the ship, you lean, and give back the kept
conversations, and in turn we tell of the years between:
you of swift Euphrates and royal Bactra and the sacred
wealth of ancient Babylon and Zeugma, the road
of the Latin peace, how sweet the grove of flowering Idyme,
where precious Tyre reddens, with what juice the purple
of Sidon is twice dyed in the vats, where in their first bud
the white twigs sweat out the lucky balsam:
but I, what tombs I gave to the conquered Pelasgians,
or what page shall close for me my laboured Thebes.

3. Consolation to Claudius Etruscus
Highest of the gods, Piety, whose most welcome power,
rare in heaven, looks upon the profaned lands,
hither, your hair filleted and distinguished by a snowy robe,
such as, present still and driven out by no fraud
of the guilty, you dwelt among rude peoples and golden realms,
come to the gentle obsequies, and behold the pious tears
of mourning Etruscus, and wipe his praised eyes.
For who, seeing him break his breast with unfilled lament
and embrace the pyre and lean upon the embers,
would not believe that the funeral of a young wife
was bewailed, or that the face of a son just growing
to manhood was snatched away by the flames? It is a father who is wept.
Be present, gods and men, at the rites; far hence, far go you guilty,
if any have an unspoken crime in their heart, and the long old age
of a wearied father, if any is conscious of a struck
mother and fears stern Aeacus at the infernal urn:
the innocent and chaste I call. See, he holds the aged
face gently clasped, and sprinkles his parent's holy
gray hair with tears, and loves the soul's last
cold; the son thinks his father's swift years
—wondrous faith!—and the dark Sisters made too much haste.
Exult, calm shades, by the Lethean streams,
rejoice, Elysian houses; lay garlands on the altars
and let festal altars gladden the pale groves.
Happy, this shade, too happy and wept by a son,
comes; far off the hisses of the Furies, far off
the threefold warder; let the long way open wide within
for excellent souls, let him go, and approach the dread
throne of the silent lord, and bear his last
thanks, and anxiously ask for the young man as many years.
A blessing on your pious groaning! We will give solace to worthy
mournings, and of our own accord we will hallow to your old man
Aonian rites of the dead, Etruscus! Lavish, plunge the Eastern
seeds, the proud harvests of Cilicia and Araby,
into the pyre; let the fire carry the heir's wealth, and from the high
mound let the cinders be packed, that will send pious clouds
to the bright sky: we will bring gifts that will not burn,
and your sorrow, with me to teach it, will endure into the coming
years. For it is not unknown to me to weep a parent;
I groaned in like fashion, flung down by the fire.
That day urges me to soothe your losses with song:
and I myself bore the complaints I now bring to you.
Not bright indeed, most gentle old man, was the line
of your race, nor a pedigree handed down from forebears, but a great
fortune supplied the lack of birth and hid the fault
of your parents. For you bore no masters from the commons,
but those whom alike the West and the East serve,
nor is that a shame to you: for what, on earth and in heaven,
remains without the law of obeying? By turns all things are ruled
and press one another by turns: every land is under
its own kings; happy Rome presses the diadems of kings;
to leaders it is given to rein her; soon their power
grows over the gods above, but even the divinities have a law:
the swift choir of the stars serves, and the wandering moon
serves, nor does the orbit of light return so many times unbidden;
and—if it be lawful now to match low things with high—
the Tirynthian too endured the harsh covenants of a savage king,
nor did the pipe of Phoebus, in service, blush.
But neither were you sent to Latium from barbarian shores:
Smyrna was your native soil, and the harbour with its reverend
spring, Meles, and the ford of Hermus, where Lydian
Bacchus enters and refreshes his horns in the golden mud.
Thence a glad sequence, and from various cares in order
honour increased; ever to walk near the divine powers, ever
to attend the side of Caesar and to cling to the gods'
sacred mysteries was granted. The Tiberian
hall first, your face scarce yet imitating a new youth,
is opened to you—here freedom, your years overcome by much
native worth, came offered—nor did the next heir,
though pitiless and driven by the Furies, drive you away.
With him too, a slender comrade even to the Arctic frosts,
you endured a tyrant dreadful in speech and look,
monstrous to his own, like those who tame the dreaded
hearts of beasts and bid them, when blood is now tasted,
give back the hands plunged in their mouths and live by no prey.
But by your merit you rose to chief deeds
when Claudius, an old man not yet dismissed to the starry
axis, passed you on to be held by a far-off heir.
Who, fearing the gods above, is granted to have deserved at once
so many temples, so many altars? The winged Arcadian
is the messenger of highest Jove; Juno wins the rain-bearing daughter of Thaumas;
swift Triton stands ready in obedience to Neptune's commands:
you so many times bore in due rite the changed yokes of leaders,
unimpaired, and your bark was happy in every deep.
And now the high day entered the pious house and Fortune,
exalted, came in with full stride; now to you alone is entrusted
the ordering of sacred wealth and the riches gathered
through all peoples and the expenses of the great world,
whatever Iberia casts out from her gold-bearing trenches,
what gleams on the Dalmatian mountain, what is swept from the African
harvests, whatever the floor of the sweltering Nile grinds,
and what the diver, sunk in the Eastern sea, gathers,
and the tilled flocks of Lacedaemonian Galaesus
and the clear snows and the Massylian timbers and the honour
of Indian ivory: to you alone, the trusted minister, all things obey
that Boreas and fierce Eurus and cloudy Auster
bring in: sooner could you count the winter rains
and the leaves of the woods. The same, watchful and of keen mind
and swift, unrolls how much under every Roman
standard by the day, and how much for the tribes, what the temples, what the high
courses of the waters, what the sea's defences
require, or the long stretched-out line of the roads;
what gold gleams on the lord's lofty ceilings,
what mass must melt, to be shaped by fire into the faces of gods,
what stamp of Ausonian Moneta rings out in the fire.
Hence for you a rare rest, and pleasure shut from your mind,
and scant feasts and care never hurt by deep
unmixed wine; yet genial laws are dear to your heart,
and to bind your mind with bridal couches and to join festive
weddings and to beget faithful clients for your lord.
Who would not know the lofty stock and the beauty of famous Etrusca?
Though by my own eyes she was not known to me,
yet a portrait gives back to fame her surpassing grace,
and the like beauty of her children shows it in their faces,
nor was her stock common; a brother bore the rods and the highest
curule chair and the Ausonian swords, and faithful
carried the appointed standards, when first the savage madness drove
the fierce Dacians on, and the race was condemned in a great triumph.
So whatever from her father's blood was lacking, the mother
restored, and the house, rejoicing in the marriage, saw the obscure
side grow bright; nor were the pledges far off;
for twice Lucina came to the births, and with light hand
herself, fertile, touched the heavy labours.
Happy—ah!—if a long day, if the just threads had granted you
to behold the faces of your children and their green cheeks!
But the joys fell broken in mid youth,
and Atropos cut with her hand the flowering years;
as the pale lilies droop their stalks
and the budding roses die at the first south winds,
or where the new purple breathes out its bloom in the spring meadows.
Around those funerals you, arrow-bearing Loves, hovered,
and anointed the pyres with the mother's balsam;
and there was no measure either with your torn wings or your hair
to scatter the fire, and the gathered quivers built the pyre.
What rites of the dead then, or what laments would you have given
to your mother's pyre, Etruscus, you who think your father's funeral
not ripe, and these years untimely for the pious!
Him too, who now with his nod tempers the high citadels,
sharing his bright offspring with the lands and the stars,
gladly endowed with the honour of an Idumaean triumph,
and, deeming him worthy of a place in the order of the victorious procession,
forbade it not, and his humble parents diminished nothing,
and the same led him down to the equestrian rows
and changed his station and stripped the ignoble iron
from his left hand and matched the honour of his sons.
Twice eight lustres flowed for his right hand,
and a course of life without a cloud, how rich for the uses
of his children, and willing to depart from his whole wealth—
witness still the splendour of lavish Etruscus, drawn from there,
to whom your indulgence gave manners not lowly.
For with embraces ever calling you back you held him,
coaxing, and never a father by command; to his honour
the brother himself too, more inclined, rejoiced to yield.
What thanks do the devoted young men render you for their reborn father,
highest of leaders, or what pious vows!
You—whether old age, slow with mould and drained of affairs,
erred, or whether coaxing Fortune long
preferred his return—were content only to warn the old man,
astonished and shuddering at the stroke of the thunderbolt to come,
with thunder and a gentle storm; and when, beyond the horrid
seas of cares, the partner went far off, leaving the Italian
fields, he was bidden to withdraw to the soft shores of the Campanian
coast and the Diomedean citadels,
and was a guest, not an exile. Nor, long delaying,
do you, Germanicus, unbar again the Romulean threshold
and cherish the mourner and raise his fallen
household. No wonder, most gentle leader, since
this is that clemency which gives the Cattians, conquered, sparing covenants,
and gives the Dacians their own mountain,
which lately, after the horrid wars, did not deem the Marcomani
and the wandering Sauromatae worthy of a Latin triumph.
And now the day is at its end, and the inexorable measure
fails. Here the devotion of sad Etruscus demands of me
such songs as neither the Sicilian rocks command
nor the swan now sure of its fate, nor the wife of savage
Tereus. Alas, with what beatings I saw him wearying
his arms, and poured out, face down, over the kisses!
Scarce do servants and companions hold him, scarce the high fire
drives him off. Not otherwise did Theseus groan along the Sunian
shores, who had deceived Aegeus with false sails.
Then, groaning fearfully and his face fouled, he addresses
the warm cinders: 'Why do you leave us, most faithful one,
with Fortune returning, father? But now we appeased the powers
of the great patron and the brief wraths of the gods above,
and you enjoy them not, and, robbed of the use of so great a gift,
you flee to the shades, ungrateful, nor is it given to bend the Fates
as to appease the harsh powers of evil Lethe.
Happy he to whom, bearing his father on his great neck,
the sacred reverence of the Mycenaean flame opened its way!
And tender Scipio, who from the savage Carthaginians
snatched his father, and the rash devotion of Lydian Lausus.
Could even the wife of the Thessalian husband weigh out
his death, and the Thracian, suppliant, conquer pitiless Styx?
How much better might this be allowed for a father!
Yet you shall not be snatched away whole, nor shall I send your funeral
far off; here your shades, here within the house I shall keep them:
you the guardian and lord of the home; to you shall all
your kin obey; I, duly the lesser and ever second,
shall pour the constant feasts and cups to your sacred
shade, and worship your image; you the bright marble,
you the line of learned wax shall give back to me like yourself,
now ivory, now tawny gold shall change your face,
thence I shall ask the way of manners and the examples of a long life
and pious addresses and dreams that will warn me.'
As he speaks such words, the father hears with glad sweetness
and slowly descends to the pitiless shades,
and bears the words to his beloved Etrusca, to tell them.
Hail for the last time, gentlest of fathers,
and for the last time farewell, who, your son surviving,
shall never suffer the sad chaos and the mournful mould of a neglected tomb.
Ever shall your altars breathe with fragrant flowers,
ever shall the happy urn drink Assyrian liquors
and tears, which is the greater honour. Here he shall offer sacrifice
to your shade, and from your own land shall raise your tomb,
and by his example deserving has consecrated to you our songs too,
rejoicing in this also, to have given even cinders to this sepulchre.

Go, locks, and cross, I pray, the easy sea;
go, reclining softly on the crowned gold;
go, gentle Cytherea will give favouring courses
and will appease the south winds; perhaps even she will carry you off
from the ship you fear, and lead you over the waters in her own shell.
Receive the praised hair, Phoebean youth,
which Caesar's boy gives to you; receive it gladly
and show it to your unshorn father, let him compare the sweet
gleaming locks and long think them his brother Lyaeus's.
Perhaps he himself too the honour of the hair that never falls
will reap and lay it for you, enclosed, in other gold.
Pergamum, far happier than pine-bearing Ida!
Though she please herself with the cloud of her sacred rape
—surely she gave to the gods above the one whom turbulent Juno
ever sees and shrinks from his hand and refuses the nectar—,
yet you, dear to the gods and marked by your beautiful nursling,
sent him to Latium, the minister whom with calm brow
Ausonian Jupiter and Roman Juno alike
look upon and both approve; nor is so great a pleasure
to the powerful lord of the lands without the gods' design.
It is said that, while she sought the Idalian groves from Eryx's summit
and golden Venus drives her soft swans,
she entered the Pergamean halls, where the greatest
helper is present to the sick, and the gentle god, staying the hastening
fates, broods over the health-bringing serpent.
Here she catches sight of a boy, brilliant with the star of surpassing
beauty, playing before the very altars of the god.
And first, a little deceived by the sudden shape,
she thinks him one of the children of the commons; but he had
no bow and no shadows from his shining shoulders.
She marvels at the boyish grace, and gazing on his face
and hair, then says: 'Will you go to the Ausonian citadels,
neglected by Venus? Will you bear the squalid roofs and the yoke
of common servitude? Far be it: I will give to that
beauty the master it has deserved. Come, go with me,
go, boy: I will lead you through the stars in my winged chariot,
a vast gift for the leader; nor shall plebeian
rights await you: you are owed to a Palatine love. Nothing,
nothing, I confess, in all the world have I seen or begotten
so sweet. The Latmian shall yield to you of his own accord
and the Sangarian boy, and he whom the empty image of the spring
and a sterile love consumed. You the dark-blue Naiad
would have preferred, and, your urn seized, would have drawn you more strongly.
You, boy, before all; he alone is more beautiful,
to whom you shall be given.' So beginning, she lifts him lightly
with her through the air and bids him sit in her swan-drawn chariot.
And no delay: now the Latian mountains and the dwellings of old
Evander, which the famous father of the world adorns
with new mass and makes Germanicus equal to the highest stars.
Then a nearer care for the goddess: what form is best
for the hair, what dress fit to kindle the rosy face,
what gold more worthy on the fingers, what on the neck.
She knew the heavenly eyes of the leader, and herself had joined
the torches and with full hand given the marriage:
so she adorns his locks, so pours the Tyrian mantle,
gives the rays and her own fire. The former delights gave way
and the troops of servants; he carries the first cups to the great
leader, and the heavy myrrh-vessels and crystal,
with a whiter hand: a new grace grows for Bacchus.
Boy dear to the gods above, chosen to taste beforehand the venerable
nectar and so often to touch the mighty hand,
which the Getae long to know, which the Persians
and Armenians and Indians long to touch! O born under a favouring
star, much has the gods' indulgence smiled on you!
Once too, lest the first down should pluck your shining
cheeks and the grace of your beautiful form should darken,
the god himself left the lofty Pergamum of his fatherland across the seas.
To no one was the power to soften the boy
entrusted, but the Phoebean youth, with silent art,
gently bids the body, shaken by no wound,
pass from its sex; yet anxious with cares
Cytherea is gnawed and fears the boy's pains.
Not yet had the leader's fair clemency begun, from his rising,
to keep males untouched; now to break the sex
and change a man is a sin, and rejoicing nature sees
only those whom she begot, nor by a sinister law
do the slave-mothers fear to bear the burdens of their sons.
You too now, a young man, had you been born later,
your cheeks shaded and stronger in your grown limbs,
would have sent no single gift, rejoicing, to the Phoebean threshold;
but now your hair alone sails to your father's shores.
This with much balsam the Paphian was saturating,
this the new Grace combed with her threefold hand;
to this the wounded hair of purple Nisus yields,
and that which swelling Achilles kept for the Spercheus.
To the boy himself, when first it was resolved to crop
his snowy brow and bare his shining shoulders with the hand,
there come the tender winged ones with the Paphian mother
and free his locks and lay the Seric mantle from his breast;
then with joined arrows they cut the hair
and set it in gold and gems; his mother herself snatches the falling
locks and Cytherea repeats the secret liquids.
Then a boy from the throng, who chanced with upturned hands
to have carried a noble mirror of jewelled gold,
'Let us give this too,' he says; 'no gift will be more welcome
to your father's temples, and more powerful than the gold itself.
Only fix your gaze and leave your face here forever.'
So he speaks and unlocked the mirror, its image seized.
But the excellent boy, stretching his palms to the stars,
'For these gifts, gentlest keeper of men,
if I have deserved it, may you renew my lord with long youth
and keep him for the world! This the stars with me,
this the waters and lands ask: let him go, I pray, through the years
of Ilium and Pylos alike, and rejoice in his own home
and let the Tarpeian temples grow old with him.'
So he speaks, and Pergamum marvels at the moved altars.

5. Eclogue to his Wife
Why so sad, tell me, why through the shared nights, wife,
anxious and sleepless, do you draw out sighs of care?
I do not fear that your faith is broken or that in that heart
is another love; against you no arrows are allowed to go
—let the Rhamnusian hear it with hostile face—it is
not allowed, and even if I myself, snatched from my native shore,
through wars, through seas for four full lustres,
should wander, you would put a thousand suitors to flight, untouched,
not feigning to unweave the cut threads,
but openly, without deceit, you would have refused the bridal chamber, armed.
Yet tell me, whence this lofty brow and clouded face?
Is it because, weary, I divine that I shall return to my Euboean
home and lay my old age to rest in my native land?
Why is this sad to you? Surely no wantonness
is in your heart, nor do the swift battles of the Circus soothe you,
nor does the crowd of the clamorous theatre enter your senses;
but honesty and shaded quiet and joys never base.
But to what waves do I snatch you as my comrade?
And yet, even if I were going to dwell beside the cold Bears,
or above the darkening shoals of Hesperian Thule,
or to the impenetrable head of the sevenfold Nile,
you would urge my ways. For yours—surely with kindly
lot Venus keeps you joined to me in my flowering years
and into old age—yours, who pierced me with my first wound
untouched by the bridal chamber and still wandering in my youth,
your reins, gladly and teachably I received,
and the bridle once set in I shall never change
but ever press; you, when I bore the Alban
gifts in my bright hair and was holily clad in Caesar's gold,
embracing me to your heart, with garlands gave
panting kisses to mine; you, when the Capitol
denied my lyre, grieved with me, conquered, over savage
and ungrateful Jove; you snatch with wakeful ear my songs
running forward at their first sounds, and whole nights
in their murmur; you alone, the witness of my long
labour, and as my Thebaid grew with your years,
such as I lately saw you, when I was snatched near the Stygian
shades, when I was hearing the Lethean streams close at hand,
and held my eyes already falling in death;
surely Lachesis, the times of my exhausted fate now spent,
pitying you alone, gave them back, and the powerful gods above
feared your envy. After all this, do you, my comrade, delay
to go on the near journey now and to the longed-for bays?
Alas, where is the known faith, tested through so many uses,
by which you match the old heroines of Latium and Greece?
To the Ilian halls Penelope would have gone, rejoicing—
for why should she let her lovers keep her?—had Ulysses suffered it;
Aegiale complained, Meliboea complained, of being left,
and she whom—how savage they were!—her beatings made a maenad.
No less than these are you. To know one faith and to give
your life to your husbands—so surely you still seek
the ashes and the former shade, so, embracing the obsequies
of your tuneful husband, you repeated the great beatings in your breast,
now mine. Nor is your devotion other, nor your care for your daughter;
so too as a mother you love, so never from your heart
does your daughter depart, and fixed in your soul's inmost shrines
you hold her night and day. Not so does the Trachinian Alcyone
circle her nests, not so does Philomela her spring dwellings,
embracing, and pour her soul into her young.
Now she holds you, because in a widowed bed alone
she now wears away the barren leisure of her lovely youth.
But they will come, the weddings will come with full torches.
So surely she deserves by the gifts of beauty and mind;
whether, embracing the lyre, she seeks it, or with her father's voice
sounds what must be learned by the Muses and shapes my songs,
or whether she parts her white arms in soft motion:
her honesty conquers her genius, her modesty her art.
Will not the light boys, will not you, Cytherea, be ashamed
that this beauty lies idle? Nor is Rome alone fertile
to reconcile the wedded couches and kindle the festive
torches: in our land too sons-in-law shall be given.
Not so far did the Vesuvian peak and the fiery storm
of the dread mountain drain the trembling cities of their citizens:
they stand and flourish with peoples; here, founded under Phoebus's
auspices, the houses of Dicarchus, and the harbour and shores
hospitable to the world; but here the tracts that imitate great Rome,
the walls that Capys filled with the Teucrians he brought,
ours too, and not rare with its own slender colonists,
Parthenope, to whom Apollo himself showed the gentle soil
across the seas with a Dionaean dove.
These seats I labour to bring you to—for neither is barbarous Thrace
nor Libya my native soil—,
seats which soft winter and cool summer temper,
which the unwarlike sea washes with sluggish waves,
where there is secure peace in the places, and the leisure of an idle life,
and quiet never disturbed, and slumbers fully slept.
No fury in the forum, nor laws drawn for quarrels:
the only law for men is the law of character, and justice without rods.
Why now should I tell of the magnificent sights and the adornments of the places,
the temples and the spaces set off by countless columns,
and the twin mass of the open and roofed theatre,
and the five-yearly games next to the Capitoline rites,
why should I praise the shore and the freedom of Menander,
which Roman dignity and Greek licence mingle?
Nor are there wanting various delights round about life:
whether the most coaxing shores, Baiae with their steam,
or to visit the inspired roofs of the prophetic Sibyl
be sweet, and the ridge memorable for the Ilian oar,
or whether the dripping vineyards of Bacchic Gaurus
and the homes of the Teleboae please you, where for trembling sailors
the Pharos lifts its sweet lights, rival of the night-wandering moon,
and the dear Surrentine ridges not poor in soft Lyaeus,
which my own dweller, Pollius, before all others enriches,
and the healing lakes of Aenaria and Stabiae reborn:
shall I recount to you a thousand loves of our land?
But enough; this, wife, it is enough to have said: it created
me for you, it bound me as your comrade for the long years.
Is not this land worthy to be seen as the mother and nurse
of us both? But I am ungrateful, who add more and doubt
your character: you will come, dearest wife,
and will even come before me; without me Tiber the lord of waters
and the roofs of arms-bearing Quirinus shall seem mean to you.
